title: Tim Cook × Starlink: iPhone Satellite Deal
summary: Negotiation on native Starlink direct-to-cell support in iPhone. Agreed on a technical pilot in the next iOS beta cycle: Starlink as a native satellite carrier option for messaging and low-rate data when terrestrial coverage drops, alongside — not replacing — Apple's existing satellite partner. Apple's conditions: full on-device privacy model, no device location retention by Starlink beyond session routing, and Apple controls the UI. Non-exclusive on both sides. Carrier-relationship messaging to be coordinated before any announcement.
decisions: Run a native Starlink direct-to-cell technical pilot in the next iOS beta cycle
Starlink joins as an additional satellite option; the existing satellite partner stays — no rip-and-replace
Starlink retains no device location data beyond live session routing; retention spec audited by Apple
Apple owns the user experience end to end; Starlink is invisible infrastructure in the UI
Deal is non-exclusive both ways; either side can add partners
Joint carrier briefing plan before any public announcement

action_items.task: Send the satellite carrier integration spec and privacy audit requirements to the Starlink team
Deliver the constellation coverage map and per-region throughput commitments for the pilot
Align the carrier-relations briefing plan with the top five carrier partners

transcript.speaker: Tim Cook
transcript.text: Elon, welcome back to Cupertino. It's been, what, two years since we sat in this room? I believe last time you threatened to build a phone.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: I threaten to build a phone roughly every eighteen months, Tim, it's a hormonal cycle at this point. The truth is I don't want to build a phone. I want the phone everyone already has to work everywhere on Earth, and you make most of the phones that matter.

transcript.speaker: Tim Cook
transcript.text: Then we want compatible things, because our satellite features are some of the most loved things we've shipped this decade. Emergency SOS has saved lives we know about by name — people write to me. But I'll let Craig say the quiet part about where we are.

transcript.speaker: Craig Federighi
transcript.text: The quiet part is capacity. Our current satellite partner got us to market first and the emergency experience is great, but it's messaging-grade capacity, and demand keeps growing past it. Meanwhile your constellation has direct-to-cell satellites overhead with two orders of magnitude more aggregate capacity. Our users don't know or care whose satellite it is. They care that the message sends.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: And that's my pitch in one sentence: Starlink as a native carrier option in iOS. When the phone loses terrestrial signal, it hands off to the constellation — messaging everywhere today, voice and app-grade data on the roadmap as we densify. No new hardware needed; we've validated with standard chipsets on the carrier partnerships we already run. The phone you shipped last year can already do this.

transcript.speaker: Tim Cook
transcript.text: We know — we've tested it, quietly, and it works better than I expected. So let me get to the real conversation, because the radio part isn't the hard part. There are three things Apple will not compromise, and I want them on the table before anyone gets excited.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Go. I've had the non-negotiables meeting twice this month already, I'm getting good at them.

transcript.speaker: Tim Cook
transcript.text: First, privacy, and this one is architectural, not contractual. A satellite carrier necessarily sees the device's position to route traffic. What it must not do is keep it. No location history, no analytics on movement, nothing retained beyond the live routing session, and we audit that — our engineers, your systems. Our users trust the phone in their pocket because we've made privacy a promise, and I will not sublet that promise to anyone. Not to you, not to anyone.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Accepted, fully. Session-scoped routing state, purged on handoff, auditable. Honestly the constellation is built that way for the government work anyway — retention is a liability for us too. Your auditors can see whatever they need under NDA. What's two?

transcript.speaker: Tim Cook
transcript.text: Two: we own the experience. There's no Starlink logo on the status bar, no Starlink app required, no upsell moments inside iOS. The user sees Apple satellite service that simply works better than before. You're infrastructure. Magnificent infrastructure — but invisible.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: This one costs me something real — the brand is worth billions and you're asking me to hide it inside your UI. But I knew it was coming, because it's exactly what I'd demand in your chair. Counter: invisible in the UI is fine, but the partnership itself is public. Announced, named, on stage. I'm not a secret supplier, Tim. The market needs to know the constellation carries iPhone traffic.

transcript.speaker: Tim Cook
transcript.text: That's fair, and frankly the announcement helps us too — it says iPhone works where nothing else does. Named partnership publicly, invisible in product. Agreed. Three is the delicate one: carriers. Our carrier partners spend tens of billions on spectrum and they are, let's say, attentive to anything that smells like Apple building a phone company around them. And you, Elon, have not historically been soothing.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: I'm extremely soothing. But the substance is on my side here: direct-to-cell runs on spectrum leased from carrier partners — the carriers are in the deal, not around it. Coverage gaps are where they lose customers and get regulator pressure; satellite fill-in makes their maps look complete. I'd frame it to them as: your network, extended, no capex.

transcript.speaker: Tim Cook
transcript.text: That's the right frame and it needs to reach them from us before it reaches them from the press. I'll take the action to brief the top five carrier partners personally — but that means nothing leaks before the briefing plan runs. Nothing. I've watched your announcement discipline from a distance, Elon, with professional concern.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: You're the third person this month to put an announcement-discipline clause on me and I've accepted all three, so at this point it's load-bearing infrastructure for my companies. Agreed — nothing public until your carrier briefings run. Craig, technical shape. What does a pilot actually look like?

transcript.speaker: Craig Federighi
transcript.text: We add Starlink as a satellite carrier profile in the next iOS beta cycle — developer beta first, behind an entitlement, maybe fifty thousand devices across the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand where your direct-to-cell coverage is densest. Messaging and location sharing first. We measure handoff reliability, latency, send-success rate against the current experience. If the numbers hold, it goes to public beta in the spring release, and voice becomes a phase-two conversation.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: The numbers will hold. Current fleet does 4.2 million direct-to-cell messages a day at 97.9 percent first-attempt delivery, and the birds launching this quarter double per-satellite capacity. I'll send you the coverage maps and signed throughput commitments per region by the 14th — real commitments, penalties attached, so your team isn't taking my word for it.

transcript.speaker: Craig Federighi
transcript.text: Penalties attached is the correct dialect for this building, thank you. One more technical item: the existing satellite partner stays. Emergency SOS keeps its current path as fallback redundancy. Two independent constellations for a life-safety feature is strictly better, and it also means this deal doesn't kill anyone's business, which matters to us.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: No objection — redundancy for emergency services is genuinely correct engineering, and I'd rather win the capacity race than the contract-law race. Non-exclusive both directions, then: you can add constellations, I keep selling direct-to-cell to Android and the carriers. The product competes on being the best, which it is.

transcript.speaker: Tim Cook
transcript.text: Non-exclusive both ways, agreed. On economics — we're not going to settle numbers today, but I want the shape agreed: Apple pays per active satellite session, not per device, with committed floors that grow with the coverage roadmap. We are very good at committed volumes, ask anyone in our supply chain. It changes lives and it also changes negotiating positions, so enjoy the honeymoon.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: I've heard legends about Apple supply-chain honeymoon endings, I'll enjoy it while it lasts. Per-session with floors works — it aligns both of us on making the service actually get used, not just installed. Our teams can fight over the decimals in September.

transcript.speaker: Tim Cook
transcript.text: Then let's recap, because I think we just did something significant. Technical pilot in the next beta cycle, four countries, messaging first. Privacy architecture with session-only routing data, audited by us. Apple owns the experience, the partnership is public but the infrastructure is invisible. Existing partner stays for emergency redundancy. Non-exclusive both ways. Per-session economics with floors, negotiated in September. And carrier briefings before a word of this leaves the room.

transcript.speaker: Craig Federighi
transcript.text: I'll have the integration spec and the privacy audit requirements to the Starlink team by the 12th. And Elon — have your team flag anything in the spec that's slow to implement now rather than in October. The beta train leaves on time. It always leaves on time.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Understood — we ship rockets on planetary schedules, we can hit an iOS beta. Tim, one closing thought: between this and what we're doing on Mars in November, there's a decent chance that within five years an iPhone works on two planets. You should put that in a keynote.

transcript.speaker: Tim Cook
transcript.text: One planet at a time, Elon. But land your robots safely in November — and if one of them takes a photo with an iPhone, I'll put it in the keynote myself.
